name: Don't Stand So Close to Me

podcast.body: A defining Police song and another top 10 hit, reaching number 10 on the Hot 100. It recounts a tale of a young, lecherous teacher's lustful feelings toward his prettiest high school pupil, drawing inspiration from Sting's past profession and Vladimir Nabokov's "Lolita," with Nabokov receiving a shout-out in the lyrics. The accompanying high-concept music video, featuring the band in caps and gowns in a classroom, was remarkably well-timed with MTV's launch. "Now, just to be clear, don't stand so close to me. Sting's tale of a young, lecherous teacher's lustful feelings toward his prettiest high school pupil is not a directly autobiographical song."

podcast.body: This early MTV hit by The Police had its melody interpolated by Sting as an "inside joke" when he sang the "I want my MTV" slogan on Dire Straits' "Money for Nothing." "Only as a bit of an inside joke, Sting sang, I want my MTV to the tune of his own early MTV hit, The Polices Don't Stand So Close To Me."

podcast.body: This song was an original hit for The Police in 1980. It was later re-recorded in 1986. "Their last recording, which would come out in the fall of 1986, after all three police members had launched solo projects, was a melancholy re-recording of their 1980 hit Don't Stand So Close To Me."

podcast.body: This melancholic re-recording of the band's 1980 hit was produced in the fall of 1986, after all three members had embarked on solo projects. It notably featured a drum machine because drummer Stuart Copeland had broken his collarbone in a horse riding accident and was unable to play the drum kit. The re-recording was included as a bonus track on their platinum-selling 1986 greatest hits compilation, "Every Breath You Take: The Singles," and peaked at number 46, missing the Top 40. "The moody re-recording featured a drum machine because Stuart Copeland had broken his collarbone in a horse riding accident and couldn't man the kit."
